doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Altissimo and confidence
summary: She works on altissimo; nervousness and biting the mouthpiece hurt it, and confidence helps.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well how did you develop the altissimo?

Well that’s one thing that also I’m still practicing because it’s not where it should be or where I would like it to be. But yeah I’m doing like overtones, doing exercises, but sometimes when I get too nervous I tend always to bite a lot of the mouthpiece and that doesn’t help the tone and the altissimo register. So that’s one thing I’m working, trying to not put so much pressure. And it’s a daily thing. Sometimes where I’m more relaxed I can go easy on altissimo and you know be more technical. If I’m nervous forget about it sometimes. I aim for a note and something else comes out. But —
Have you ever experienced the fact that you go for some of those notes in the practice room and you can’t get them but when you’re surrounded by friendly chords that they seem to come out?
I’m not sure what that’s about.

Well you know I — the more I’m getting older I realize that it has to do a lot with confidence. There is something that if you feel at ease with the musicians you don’t feel to prove yourself, if you just say I’m here to do what I can do and I do the best and I’ll try to have fun. Sometimes everything works better. If you just start to kind of double- guessing yourself, wondering what people might think, getting nervous, that’s a recipe for disaster, at least for me. You know sometimes I finish the gig, one of those stressful gigs that you just say you feel you have — like you’re trying to impress or at least, I don’t know, getting all into the what they’re thinking. And I always think oh my God thanks God I’m not a surgeon I would have killed somebody tonight. So at least I can relax on that.
